extracted.intended_audience: public relations / communications professionals and press-release authors
extracted.subtask_description: A Bernays-informed rubric to judge whether a press release is worth issuing — i.e., whether it is likely to be picked up — based on campaign architecture, audience research, intermediaries, symbolism, and ethics rather than copy alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the release the product of "thorough knowledge of the situation and the application of scientific principles" — i.e., grounded in research on the receiving audience — rather than a generic announcement?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the release was designed from research/segmentation/insight about the target audience and media ecosystem. Anti-patterns: one-size-fits-all boilerplate releases issued without audience analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group-leader leverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release work through opinion leaders and intermediary group leaders (medical-society heads, academic deans, civic-association presidents) rather than appealing directly to the mass?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer releases that enlist or foreground endorsing authorities and intermediaries; releases that only address the masses directly are weaker per Bernays. Check for named endorsers or evidence of outreach to intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive-aligned themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the themes in the release tied to motives the audience already holds (health, status, security, family) rather than to the issuer's internal motives (revenue, reputation)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether messaging frames the announcement in terms of audience-relevant motives. Anti-patterns: messaging focused on the issuer's convenience, profits, or internal milestones without translating to audience benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactured organisation of consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Has a coalition, council, association, or coordinated event been assembled so the release can announce a collective position rather than a single voice?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of alliances, joint statements, or organized events that let the announcement read as a collective endorsement. Single-firm solo announcements are less likely to persuade or be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Are abstract programs reduced to single concrete symbols (a torch, a march, a "first of its kind") that journalists can carry in a headline?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether complex ideas are tied to a simple, memorable symbol or image for easy press translation and headlineability. Absence of a strong symbol reduces pickup likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirection
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release advance the client's interest by means of an apparently independent third action (a survey, a contest, an award, a holiday)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the announcement is framed as coming from or enabled by a seemingly neutral or third-party activity. Such indirection increases credibility and journalist interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous campaign frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this release a planned beat in an ongoing campaign rather than an isolated event? Bernays argues sustained engineering, not one-shot announcements, moves opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer releases that fit into a documented cadence or campaign plan; single-shot releases should be rare and only used when genuinely newsworthy on their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for the "invisible government"
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release acknowledge — and try to mobilize — the network of intermediaries (associations, institutes, academic figures) who actually shape what filters through?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether outreach and messaging strategy consider institutional gatekeepers and networks. Releases that ignore intermediaries underestimate how news and opinion are formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release treat the public as competent receivers whose attention must be actively earned, or as passive recipients? (Bernays's view: "conscious and intelligent manipulation of organized habits" is necessary in democratic society.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the release makes a case for why active engineering is required to inform or mobilize the public; avoid paternalistic or trivializing tones that assume passive uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical screen
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release pass the test that the advocacy side could be defended in public if its mechanisms were disclosed? (Bernays acknowledges propaganda's ethical valence depends on point of view.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a transparency/defensibility check: would the coalition, methods, and intent withstand public scrutiny? Use this as an ethical veto or modifier when deciding to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-worthiness implication (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highest-pickup releases typically: (a) come from a coalition rather than a single firm, (b) align with motives editors attribute to their audiences, (c) bring a pre-staged endorsing voice along with the announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three predictors as a quick checklist when triaging potential releases. If a release meets none of (a)-(c), its likelihood of editorial pickup is low regardless of writing quality.
